catalog_quote: [Terrill 1998, sec. 2.7, p. 13, Google Books scan excerpt] 2.7 STRESS Primary stress falls on the first syllable of a word . Secondary stress falls on the third syllable if present . [Holmer 1983, Part II, p. 178] 2.11 Word or syllable stress is not significant in any of the languages studied here. The spoken context runs smooth without emphasis of any syllable unless in cases of long vowels (or diphthongs), besides not very frequent in the Gunggari languages. As usual, in a spoken context or sequence of syllables, however, the second initial syllable often carries mechanically more stress than the others (cf. in Part I, 2.9), which explains the origin of such shortened forms as ḑe· (Gun EA) for jinḑia where?; this tendency is frequently reflected in the current pronunciation of place names of several syllables, derived from Aboriginal words, in Queensland: Barálba, Mundúbbera etc. [Holmer 1983, Part I, p. 5] 2.9 Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey. Still a certain tendency persists everywhere to stress the vowel of the second initial syllable in words or utterances of some length ...

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Opened (18 pp., pypdf extract of) and rendered extract p. 3 = PL-D54 p. 178 (saved). Section 2.11 is there word for word as quoted; the only differences are typographic: the page prints the stressed syllable of the place names (Barálba, Mundúbbera), writes 'jinḑia' with a hooked palatal d (the quote has 'jingia', from the scanned), and 'ge·' with the length dot. Part I 2.9 p. 5 (extract p. 2) also matches the report: 'Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey. Still a certain tendency persists everywhere to stress the vowel of the second initial syllable in words or utterances of some length'. In the full text the same claim recurs for Bidjara 8.5 p.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Holmer (the only first-hand source opened): stress is not significant (not distinctive) in Gangulu or any other language of his Gunggari group; in connected speech or longer words the second syllable tends to carry more prominence than the others ('second initial syllable' = second syllable from the start), with, per his Bidjara remark (8.5, p. 205), secondary stress on subsequent alternate syllables. This CONTRADICTS the modern primary description, Terrill 1998 Biri sec. 2.7 STRESS (seen only in a Google Books snippet, page not visible): 'Primary stress falls on the first syllable of a word. Secondary stress falls on the third syllable if present.' Terrill also remarks (per a McGregor 2008 snippet) that Holmer's phonological analysis 'was unusual'. Reviewer should weigh Holmer's not-significant/second-syllable claim against Terrill's initial-stress rule for Biri incl. Gangulu.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Holmer: none stated for Gangulu; group-level 'second initial syllable.. carries mechanically more stress' and, in the Bidjara section (8.5, p. 205), 'secondary stress appearing on subsequent alternate syllables'. Terrill 1998 sec. 2.7 (snippet): secondary stress on the third syllable if present.
new_statements.exceptions: Holmer: syllables with long vowels or diphthongs are emphasised (long vowels are infrequent in the Gunggari languages); the second-syllable tendency is invoked to explain aphaeretic shortenings (ge· < jingia 'where?') and the English pronunciation of Queensland place names (Baralba, Mundubbera).
new_statements.domain_note: Holmer's statement concerns word or syllable stress and 'the spoken context', i.e. both word and phrase level, for elicited salvage material recorded 1970-72 from six Gangulu informants (three Gangulu A, three Gangulu B). Terrill 1998's snippet statement is about the word ('first syllable of a word').
new_statements.identity_note: Holmer 1983 describes 'Gangulu (A)' (Nebo/Springsure, western-northern) and 'Gangulu (B)' (Woorabinda/Rockhampton, eastern) from six informants, pp. 267-281, as one of the seven languages of his 'Gunggari group'; his stress statement (Part II 2.11) is made for that whole group, not for Gangulu alone. Terrill 1998 (Biri, Lincom) treats Gangulu as a dialect of Biri (Glottolog biri1256), so her stress statement (seen only in a Google Books snippet) is for the Biri language as a whole, with Gangulu as 'the best represented dialect after Biri' per her own snippet.

readall_conflicts: The pre-existing tension stands unchanged: the catalog's fixed-unreviewed initial-stress rule (initial stress, world-r2-2026-09-17, resting on the Terrill 1998 Biri snippet "Primary stress falls on the first syllable of a word. Secondary stress falls on the third syllable if present", page unverified) versus Holmer 1983 (PL-D54, Part II sec. 2.11, p. 178; Part I sec. 2.9, p. 5), who says word or syllable stress is not significant in any of the Gunggari-group languages including Gangulu, with only a mechanical tendency for the second initial syllable to carry more stress. The Tindale (1974) forms Breen quotes on p. 238 (['bama], ['ka:ŋu] for Kangulu) carry initial stress marks and are consistent with the catalog's initial reading, but they are two quoted disyllables from a tribal catalogue, not evidence of a rule, and they do not resolve the Terrill/Holmer disagreement.
